questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.stem: Ines's tank notes begin by asking what a critical essay claims, and she writes that such an essay argues for a reading rather than a summary.

options.text: A critical essay argues for a reading and defends it, so its claims are readings, not description.
A critical essay states facts about a work and lets the reader draw the interpretation from them.
options.misconception: treats interpretation as something a reader supplies alone

options.text: A critical essay reports what critics have already said, and its contribution is the order of the summaries.
options.misconception: reduces the essay to an arrangement of other people's views

options.text: A critical essay states its conclusions first, so that a reader can decide whether the rest is worth reading.
options.misconception: believes the conclusion should come before the argument

questions.explanation: A critical essay makes an interpretable claim and defends it against rivals, so the reader is being asked to agree or disagree. B, C and D each replace that with a different and weaker job for the form.
questions.hint: Ask what the essay asks the reader to accept.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An inconsistency claim against a writing claim
questions.learningObjective: Separate an inconsistency claim from a writing claim
questions.stem: Tuan's note distinguishes a claim that a text contradicts itself from a claim that its prose is badly written.

answer.exemplar: An inconsistency claim and a writing claim point at different things. Inconsistency means the work says two things that cannot both be held, which is a claim about what the work asserts and can be shown by placing the two passages side by side. A writing claim says the sentences are badly made, which is a judgement about execution and depends on criteria the critic must supply. The first can be checked by a reader; the second has to be argued.

questions.explanation: The first claim is about what the work asserts and can be checked by a reader; the second is about execution and needs criteria supplied. Confusing them lets a stylistic verdict pass as a logical one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the work contradicts itself or is badly made.

questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.stem: Marisol writes that an essay beginning with her own flooded garage should not draw general conclusions from one case.

options.text: The essay should not have used the garage, since personal material carries a general claim on its own.
options.misconception: believes personal material supports a general claim by itself

options.text: The personal sets the scene but cannot carry the general claim, which needs evidence beyond one experience.
The essay should generalise confidently, since a writer's own case is the strongest evidence a reader can have.
options.misconception: treats one case as the strongest possible evidence

options.text: The essay should cut the garage, since an opening about property damage offends readers of criticism.
options.misconception: judges an opening by its subject rather than by its work

questions.explanation: The personal can establish the writer's situation and give the argument its ground, but a claim about a general pattern needs evidence from beyond one life. A, C and D each misjudge what the example can carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the personal establishes and what it cannot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Letting an unfair sentence stand
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an unfair sentence should stand

stimulus.body: Draft sentence, 6 August: most marine biologists who work with tanks are poor at writing, which is why the field's public voice is so bad. I have read this in a review once. It is sharp. I am not sure it is fair, and I cannot say it is not, because nobody has shown me it is unfair.

questions.stem: What is the problem with leaving this sentence as drafted?

options.text: There is no problem, because a sharp sentence is what keeps a reader awake in a critical essay.
options.misconception: values sharpness over the warrant for a general claim

options.text: There is no problem, because the writer attributes the view to someone who published it elsewhere.
options.misconception: releases the writer by attributing the view to another source

options.text: It makes an unevidenced general claim about a group, and unfairness has not been established.
The only problem is length, because the sentence should be broken into two before it appears in a draft.
options.misconception: redirects the fault from the claim to the sentence's length

questions.explanation: The sentence generalises about a whole group on no stated evidence, and the writer has not shown it to be unfair either. Sharpness, attribution and line length do not settle a claim of that reach.
questions.hint: Ask how much the sentence claims.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a reflective opening supplies
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a reflective opening supplies
questions.stem: An essay in the tank notebook opens by describing the biologist's first failed attempt to keep an anemone alive.

answer.exemplar: A reflective opening supplies a position the rest of the essay can argue from: it shows the writer's situation, what she expected, and what actually happened, so that a reader can see the claim growing out of an experience rather than arriving ready-made. The failure here does not prove anything about marine biology; it gives the reader the ground on which the essay's later argument stands, and makes the argument answerable to the writer's own case.

questions.explanation: The opening shows the writer's expectation meeting an outcome, which gives the reader the ground the argument stands on. It does not by itself establish anything general; it establishes where the claim comes from.
questions.hint: Ask what ground the argument stands on.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An instance that carries an abstraction
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether an instance carries its abstraction
questions.stem: A line in the tank notebook cites one hermit crab's choice of shell to support a claim about how animals trade comfort for safety.

answer.exemplar: An instance carries an abstraction when it is selected because it shows the general pattern rather than because it is striking on its own, and the reader can see why it was chosen. The shell choice works as an instance if the essay says what general habit it exemplifies and what would count against it. Chosen for colour or surprise, the same crab proves nothing at all, and a reader who cannot see the selection has been shown a fact rather than an argument.

questions.explanation: An instance carries an abstraction when the reader can see why it was chosen and what it exemplifies. Without that, it is a vivid fact, and vividness is not evidence for the claim it is attached to.
questions.hint: Say why this instance was chosen.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.stem: A personal essay in the tank notebook uses the writer's own failed tank to argue that all public aquaria hide their failures.

answer.exemplar: The personal can establish that a failure happened and can show how the writer felt about it, but a single instance cannot establish that every institution behaves the same way. To move from one tank to all public aquaria the essay would need evidence beyond the writer's own, such as published budgets, inspection reports, or the accounts of people who have seen them run. Without that the move is a wish rather than a conclusion, however honestly the story is told.

questions.explanation: One failure can ground the essay in lived experience, but the general claim needs evidence from outside it. Without that, the essay has a true story and a conclusion it has not earned.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence the general claim needs.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a reflective opening supplies
questions.stem: A reflective opening in the tank notebook describes the writer watching a crab rearrange its shell for an hour before the essay begins its argument.

answer.exemplar: A reflective opening supplies the situation and the expectation behind the argument, so that the reader can see the claim as a response to something rather than as an assertion. What the opening cannot do is begin to prove anything; it can only establish where the argument came from.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.stem: A note in the tank notebook asks whether a critical essay's central claim should be about a work's meaning or about its construction.

answer.exemplar: The two kinds of claim do different work in an essay. A claim about meaning asks a reader to accept an interpretation of what the work says, and it must be argued by showing that the reading accounts for the details better than its rivals. A claim about construction asks how the work was made, and it can be checked against the evidence of its making. An essay that slides between them can sound forceful while proving nothing, because each kind of claim requires a different kind of support.

questions.explanation: Meaning claims must be argued against rival readings; construction claims can be checked against evidence of how the work was made. Sliding between them produces confidence without support.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of support the claim needs.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.stem: One personal essay in the tank notebook uses the writer's own diagnosis to argue that marine biology careers are unfairly structured.

answer.exemplar: The limit of the personal is not that it cannot carry argument but that it cannot carry a claim about how a whole field works. A writer's own experience establishes what happened to that writer and can be offered as evidence of how it felt, but a general claim about careers needs more than one life in it: records, statistics, or the accounts of others in the same position. The personal establishes the standpoint; it does not supply the survey.

questions.explanation: The personal establishes the writer's standpoint and their experience, but a claim about a whole field needs evidence from beyond one life. The personal supplies where the argument stands, not its survey.
questions.hint: Ask what the personal establishes and what it cannot.

questions.topic: An opening that supplies no context
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an opening that supplies no context
questions.stem: An essay's opening names the writer's grandmother and the pond she kept, and then moves straight to an argument about public water policy.

answer.exemplar: An opening that supplies no context gives the reader a name and an image but nothing to do with them, so the argument that follows has to be taken on its own terms and the reader has no way to connect the two. Without it the opening is decoration and the essay has to start its argument twice, once here and once there.

questions.explanation: The opening provides image without relevance, so it neither grounds the argument nor supports it. Context would make the transition a move the reader can follow rather than a jump.

questions.topic: What kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.stem: Ines writes that a critical essay's claims must be arguable by someone who disagrees, and she checks her own sentences against that test.

answer.exemplar: A claim of the kind a critical essay makes is not a fact about the text but an interpretation of it, and it is interpretable because a reader could decline it. That test does not make claims timid or provisional in tone; it makes them specific, because a claim that nobody could deny is not saying anything a reader needs to think about. Checking each sentence against the test is how a writer discovers which sentences are doing real work and which are only sounding like argument.

questions.explanation: Testing a claim for arguability separates interpretation from summary, and it catches sentences that sound like argument without being disputable. The test sharpens claims rather than weakening them.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could decline the claim.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Letting an unfair sentence stand
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an unfair sentence should stand
questions.stem: A draft in the tank notebook calls an essayist's work careless, and the supporting material is one misplaced word in a fifty-page essay.

answer.exemplar: An unfair sentence is one whose claim outruns its support, and the support has to match the size of the claim. A single misplaced word is a real fault and can be described precisely as a slip, but calling fifty pages careless would make the reader think the carelessness is general. The writer's options are to keep the sentence, report the slip for what it is, or drop it; what cannot be done is to use a small fault to imply a general one and trust the reader to notice the difference.

questions.explanation: The detail is genuine but narrow, while the word applied is general. Letting it stand asserts a pattern the evidence cannot support, and the honest options are to describe the slip accurately or drop it.
questions.hint: Ask how large the fault really is.

questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.stem: One essay in the tank notebook claims that the writer's own year of night shifts shows how institutions really work.

answer.exemplar: The personal reports the writer's experience accurately and can explain why an institution looked the way it did from the inside, which is a contribution no outside account easily matches. It cannot by itself establish how institutions work in general, because one year in one building is one case, and the essay's own evidence shows that its writer knows the difference between seeing and generalising. The personal therefore supports the claim about that place, and the wider claim has to be argued from more than it.

questions.explanation: The personal explains an institution from the inside and supports a claim about that one place, but a general claim needs more cases than the writer's own. The limit is where the personal stops and the survey begins.
questions.hint: Ask how many cases the personal supplies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Letting an unfair sentence stand
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an unfair sentence should stand
questions.stem: A draft says an essayist's work is lazy, and supports this with one paragraph the writer calls thin.

options.text: The judgement holds, because a thin paragraph is exactly what laziness in prose looks like.
options.misconception: reads a single weakness as evidence of a general quality

options.text: The judgement holds, because the draft names the evidence, which is what a reader needs in order to check it.
options.misconception: treats naming the evidence as sufficient support

options.text: The judgement holds, because the word lazy is a plain one and plain words need less support.
options.misconception: believes plain words carry less evidential weight

options.text: The judgement outruns the evidence, since one thin paragraph cannot show laziness across a body of work.

questions.explanation: The word claims a settled habit and the evidence shows one paragraph, so the sentence asserts a pattern the draft has not established. Symptom, citation and plainness are all offered in place of the support the charge requires.
questions.hint: Ask how far the paragraph reaches.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a reflective opening supplies
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a reflective opening supplies

stimulus.body: Draft opening, 19 July. My grandmother kept eels in a barrel behind the shed. I never asked her why she kept them, and she never said. The rest of this essay is about what I did not ask her, and what that silence has cost me as a reader of my own family's accounts of where we came from.

questions.stem: Which judgement best describes this opening?

options.text: It supplies the situation, the silence and the question the essay pursues, letting the argument answer it.
It supplies an abstraction, since the barrel is introduced to stand for a general kind of family silence.
options.misconception: treats the concrete image as an illustration of a prior idea

options.text: It supplies only atmosphere, since the grandmother is scenery for the essay's later general claim.
options.misconception: reduces the opening to scenery for a later claim

options.text: It supplies evidence for the claim, because a grandmother who kept eels is typical of the coastal families.
options.misconception: takes one family's practice as typical without evidence

questions.explanation: The opening gives the reader the scene, the unanswered question and the essay's purpose, which is what lets the later argument answer something live. Abstraction, atmosphere and typicality each miss that work.
questions.hint: Ask what the opening makes available.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An opening that supplies no context
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an opening that supplies no context
questions.stem: A tank-note essay opens with a general claim that institutions value appearance over substance, and does not return to it until its last page.

answer.exemplar: An opening that supplies no context supplies a verdict in place of an argument, and a verdict the essay does not return to for thirty pages leaves the reader carrying it unexamined. A general claim about institutions cannot be checked against anything the essay has yet given them, so it functions as a tone-setter rather than as a thesis. The essay would be stronger if it either made the claim specific enough to test early, or postponed it until it had the evidence to earn it.

questions.explanation: A general claim given first and never examined functions as a verdict, not a thesis, and it makes the reader carry an unargued premise. Making it specific or postponing it until the evidence is in hand would fix it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim could be checked yet.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An instance that carries an abstraction
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether an instance carries its abstraction
questions.stem: One tank note uses a single recorded tank reading to illustrate the essay's larger claim about intervention in living systems.

options.text: The instance carries the abstraction, because a real measurement is more persuasive than an abstract assertion.
options.misconception: prefers concreteness to relevance

options.text: The instance carries the abstraction only if the note says what it exemplifies and what would refute it.
The instance carries the abstraction, because the reading is the part of the essay most likely to be checked.
options.misconception: values verifiability of the example over its relevance

options.text: The instance carries the abstraction, because a single case is the clearest way to show that something happens at all.
options.misconception: treats any single case as adequate support for a general claim

questions.explanation: An instance carries a general claim only when the note says what it exemplifies and what would count against it. Persuasiveness, verifiability and sheer concreteness are all substitutes for that statement.
questions.hint: Ask what the instance has to say.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.stem: A tank notebook asks what makes a claim arguable, and Ines checks each sentence of her draft against that test.

answer.exemplar: A claim of the kind a critical essay makes is not a fact about the text but an interpretation of it, and it is interpretable because a reader could decline it. That test does not make claims timid or provisional in tone; it makes them specific, because a claim that nobody could deny is not saying anything a reader needs to think about. Checking each sentence against the test is how a writer discovers which sentences are doing real work and which are only sounding like argument.

questions.explanation: Testing a claim for arguability separates interpretation from summary, and it catches sentences that sound like argument without being disputable. The test sharpens claims rather than weakening them.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could decline the claim.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An inconsistency claim against a writing claim
questions.learningObjective: Separate an inconsistency claim from a writing claim
questions.stem: A tank-note essay argues that a novel's two accounts of the same reef cannot both be true, and supports the claim with two lines quoted side by side.

options.text: The claim overstates the evidence, because two accounts of a reef can differ without either being false.
options.misconception: assumes any difference of description defeats a contradiction claim

options.text: The claim holds, because quoting the two lines side by side is all a reader needs to confirm it.
options.misconception: treats the presentation of evidence as sufficient proof

options.text: The claim holds, because setting the two assertions out lets a reader check the conflict for themselves.
The claim is really about prose, since the difficulty of the two lines is what the reader will notice.
options.misconception: redirects the claim to style instead of testing the conflict

questions.explanation: Setting the two assertions side by side is what lets a reader see the conflict and confirm it for themselves, which is the form an inconsistency claim must take. Difference of description, citation alone and difficulty of phrasing all miss the point.
questions.hint: Ask how the reader confirms the conflict.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of the personal in a personal essay

stimulus.body: I have been asked to write about the year I spent as a night porter in a marine station, and I keep drifting into telling readers that porters hold institutions together. That is not what I know. I know that I was there, that the tanks were fed at three, and that without the night shift the work stopped. The rest is a story I like about myself.

questions.stem: What limit on the personal does this log entry recognise?

options.text: The account supports what one porter observed; the general claim would be a story, not knowledge.
The entry suggests the writer is not qualified to write about marine stations, since porters do not qualify.
options.misconception: treats a lack of formal qualification as disqualifying from writing

options.text: The entry suggests the personal material is worthless, since a night porter's observations carry no authority.
options.misconception: dismisses first-hand observation as lacking authority

options.text: The entry suggests the writer should abandon the personal essay and report the feeding schedule instead.
options.misconception: redirects the writer to another subject instead of a narrower claim

questions.explanation: The entry separates what the writer knows, the tanks fed at three, from the flattering story about porters, which is exactly the limit the personal imposes. Qualification, authority and subject change do not describe the problem the writer identifies.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer knows and what it cannot show.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Letting an unfair sentence stand
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an unfair sentence should stand
questions.stem: A tank-note draft says an earlier writer was careless, and the evidence is that the writer once spelled a scientific name wrongly in a footnote.

answer.exemplar: The charge of carelessness is general and the evidence is a single slip in a footnote, and no reader will think those the same size. The honest options are to keep the word and add the qualification, to report the slip as the slip it is, or to drop it, and each changes what the essay is claiming. What cannot be done is to let the general word stand on the narrow evidence and trust the reader to weigh them the way the writer would have liked.

questions.explanation: A general word resting on a single narrow slip asks the reader to make an inference the evidence does not support. Reporting the slip accurately, or dropping it, keeps the essay's claims honest.
questions.hint: Ask how much the word claims.
